title: Decision Trees II - Entropy, Gini and Information Gain
abstract:
How a tree decides which question to ask. Entropy and the Gini index measure how
impure a node is; information gain measures how much a candidate split
reduces that impurity; and the tree greedily takes the split with the highest
gain. This document derives both impurity measures, explains the ranges the notes
give ($[0,1]$ for entropy, $[0,0.5]$ for Gini), works the notes' Outlook example
end to end, contrasts ID3 with CART, and covers the bias towards high-cardinality
features that gain ratio was invented to fix.

The ranges are for two classes

Entropy's maximum is $\log_2 C$ for $C$ classes, so it is $1$ for binary,
$\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ for three classes. Gini's maximum is $1-1/C$, so $0.5$
for binary and $0.667$ for three. The notes' ranges are the binary case, which is
the one you meet most.

items:
High entropy means an unordered set — e.g. it is
 hard to predict the next card in an unordered deck.

Low entropy means an ordered set — e.g. it is
 easy to predict the next card in an ordered deck.

blocks.t:
$H$ is the average number of yes/no questions needed to identify the class of a
random member of the node.

items: All one class: you already know. $0$ questions, $H=0$.
50/50: you need exactly one question. $H=1$ bit.
Four equally likely classes: two questions. $H=2$ bits.

blocks.t: That is why the base of the logarithm is 2, and why the unit is bits.

Conceptually the same as entropy at node level. Only the mathematical
formulas are different. Slightly faster than entropy.

$G$ is the probability that two items drawn at random from the node have
different labels — equivalently, the probability of misclassifying an
item if you labelled it by drawing at random from the node's own distribution.
Zero when the node is pure; maximal when the classes are balanced.

blocks.cap:
Left: both measures are zero at the pure ends and maximal at
 $p=0.5$, differing only in scale. Middle: the timing difference the notes
 mention — entropy's logarithm is measurably slower. Right: normalised, the two

blocks.t:
scikit-learn defaults to criterion="gini", and the choice almost never
changes the resulting tree meaningfully — the curves are that similar. Use Gini
unless you have a specific reason (information-theoretic interpretation, or
compatibility with a published ID3 result).

Information Gain — choose which feature to use for splitting.
It measures how good a feature is at reducing the entropy.
Whichever feature has higher IG, use that to split the tree.
The decision tree chooses the split with the largest entropy reduction.

The subtracted term is the weighted average impurity of the children —
weighted by how many rows land in each. Weighting matters: a perfectly pure child
containing two rows is worth far less than a nearly pure child containing two
hundred.
$IG\ge0$ always, and $IG=0$ means the split told you nothing.

CART (Classification \
Regression Trees)
rows: Very common — the basis of Random Forest

blocks.t:
A multiway split on a categorical feature with $k$ levels creates $k$ children at
once, exhausting the feature in a single step and fragmenting the data. CART's
binary splits ask "is $x_j\in A$?" and can revisit the same feature further
down, which uses the data far more efficiently. Binary trees are also simpler to
implement, to prune and to make numeric — which is why scikit-learn implements
CART and not ID3, and why every modern boosting library is binary too.
Information gain prefers features with many distinct values

A feature with many levels can split the data into many small, accidentally pure
groups. In the extreme, a unique ID column gives $IG = H(S)$ — the maximum
possible — and is completely useless for prediction.

items:
Gain ratio (C4.5, ID3's successor): divide $IG$ by the
 split information $-\sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\log_2\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}$,
 which penalises splits producing many branches.

Binary splits (CART): a two-way split cannot fragment the data
 into $k$ pieces at once, which mitigates the problem structurally.

blocks.t:
The same bias contaminates impurity-based feature importance (Topic 63),
which is why permutation importance is preferred when the features have very
different cardinalities.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# =====================================================================
# 1. ENTROPY AND GINI
# =====================================================================
def entropy(counts):
    c = np.asarray(counts, dtype=float)
    c = c[c > 0]                                  # 0*log(0) = 0 by convention
    p = c / c.sum()
    return float(-(p * np.log2(p)).sum())

def gini(counts):
    c = np.asarray(counts, dtype=float)
    p = c / c.sum()
    return float(1 - (p ** 2).sum())

print(f"{'node':>16s} {'p':>6s} {'entropy':>9s} {'gini':>7s}  reading")
for counts, note in [([10, 0],  "pure"),
                     ([9, 1],   "nearly pure"),
                     ([7, 3],   "mixed"),
                     ([5, 5],   "MAXIMUM impurity"),
                     ([1, 9],   "nearly pure (other class)")]:
    p = counts[0] / sum(counts)
    print(f"{str(counts):>16s} {p:6.2f} {entropy(counts):9.4f} "
          f"{gini(counts):7.4f}  {note}")
# Entropy range [0,1], Gini range [0,0.5] -- both 0 when pure, max at p=0.5.

# The ranges depend on the number of CLASSES:
for C in [2, 3, 4, 8]:
    balanced = [1] * C
    print(f"{C} balanced classes: entropy {entropy(balanced):.4f} "
          f"(max log2({C}) = {np.log2(C):.4f}), gini {gini(balanced):.4f} "
          f"(max 1-1/{C} = {1-1/C:.4f})")

# ENTROPY IS A NUMBER OF QUESTIONS:
print(f"\n4 equally likely classes -> {entropy([1,1,1,1]):.0f} yes/no questions")
print(f"2 equally likely classes -> {entropy([1,1]):.0f} yes/no question")
print(f"1 class                  -> {entropy([1,0]):.0f} questions (you know already)")

# =====================================================================
# 2. WHY GINI IS FASTER -- the notes' claim, measured
# =====================================================================
import time
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
p = rng.random(2_000_000)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
_ = -p*np.log2(p) - (1-p)*np.log2(1-p)
t_ent = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
_ = 1 - (p**2 + (1-p)**2)
t_gini = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"\nentropy {t_ent:.4f}s   gini {t_gini:.4f}s   "
      f"({t_ent/t_gini:.1f}x)   -- the log is the cost")

# =====================================================================
# 3. INFORMATION GAIN -- the notes' Outlook example, in full
# =====================================================================
data = pd.DataFrame({
    "Outlook":     ["Sunny"]*5 + ["Overcast"]*4 + ["Rain"]*5,
    "Temperature": ["Hot","Hot","Mild","Cool","Mild",
                    "Hot","Cool","Mild","Hot",
                    "Mild","Cool","Cool","Mild","Mild"],
    "Humidity":    ["High","High","High","Normal","Normal",
                    "High","Normal","High","Normal",
                    "High","Normal","Normal","Normal","High"],
    "Windy":       [False,True,False,False,True,
                    False,True,True,False,
                    False,False,True,False,True],
    "Play":        ["No","No","No","Yes","Yes",
                    "Yes","Yes","Yes","Yes",
                    "Yes","Yes","No","Yes","No"],
})

def counts_of(sub):
    return sub.Play.value_counts().values

root_H = entropy(counts_of(data))
print(f"\nroot: {dict(data.Play.value_counts())}  H = {root_H:.4f}")

def information_gain(df, feature, impurity=entropy):
    total = len(df)
    weighted = 0.0
    rows = []
    for v, sub in df.groupby(feature):
        w = len(sub) / total
        imp = impurity(counts_of(sub))
        weighted += w * imp
        rows.append((v, dict(sub.Play.value_counts()), len(sub), imp))
    return impurity(counts_of(df)) - weighted, weighted, rows

ig, after, rows = information_gain(data, "Outlook")
print("\nsplitting on Outlook:")
for v, cnt, n, h in rows:
    tag = "  <- PURE (leaf node)" if h == 0 else "  <- impure, split again"
    print(f"  {v:9s} {str(cnt):22s} n={n}  H={h:.4f}{tag}")
print(f"weighted child entropy = {after:.4f}")
print(f"IG(Outlook) = {root_H:.4f} - {after:.4f} = {ig:.4f}")

# EVERY feature, and the winner:
print(f"\n{'feature':>13s} {'IG (entropy)':>14s} {'IG (gini)':>11s}")
for f in ["Outlook", "Temperature", "Humidity", "Windy"]:
    a = information_gain(data, f, entropy)[0]
    b = information_gain(data, f, gini)[0]
    star = "  <- HIGHEST, split on this" if f == "Outlook" else ""
    print(f"{f:>13s} {a:14.4f} {b:11.4f}{star}")
# Both criteria agree that Outlook is best -- as they almost always do.

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE WEIGHTING MATTERS
# =====================================================================
# A pure child of 2 rows is worth far less than a nearly pure child of 200.
print(f"\nsplit A: children [2 pure] and [12 mixed 9/3]")
print(f"  weighted = {2/14*entropy([2,0]) + 12/14*entropy([9,3]):.4f}")
print(f"split B: children [7 mixed 6/1] and [7 mixed 3/4]")
print(f"  weighted = {7/14*entropy([6,1]) + 7/14*entropy([3,4]):.4f}")
# Without the |S_v|/|S| weights, split A would look better than it is.

# =====================================================================
# 5. sklearn AGREES
# =====================================================================
X = pd.get_dummies(data.drop(columns="Play")).astype(int)
y = data.Play

for crit in ["entropy", "gini"]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion=crit, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
    root_feat = X.columns[t.tree_.feature[0]]
    print(f"\ncriterion={crit:8s} root split on: {root_feat}")
    print(f"  impurity at root: {t.tree_.impurity[0]:.4f}")
# Both pick an Outlook dummy. Note sklearn is CART, so the split is BINARY
# ("Outlook_Overcast <= 0.5") rather than the 3-way split of ID3.

print("\n", export_text(DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", max_depth=2,
                                               random_state=0).fit(X, y),
                        feature_names=list(X.columns)))

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE CARDINALITY BIAS -- IG loves useless ID columns
# =====================================================================
n = 500
df2 = pd.DataFrame({
    "row_id":  np.arange(n),                       # a UNIQUE id: useless
    "useful":  rng.integers(0, 2, n),
    "coarse":  rng.integers(0, 3, n),
})
df2["Play"] = np.where(df2.useful == 1, "Yes", "No")   # truth = 'useful' only

for f in ["row_id", "useful", "coarse"]:
    g = information_gain(df2.rename(columns={"Play": "Play"}), f)[0]
    print(f"IG({f:8s}) = {g:.4f}   ({df2[f].nunique()} distinct values)")
# row_id gets the MAXIMUM possible gain and predicts nothing on new data.

# GAIN RATIO divides by the split information, penalising many branches:
def gain_ratio(df, feature):
    ig = information_gain(df, feature)[0]
    props = df[feature].value_counts(normalize=True).values
    split_info = -(props * np.log2(props)).sum()
    return ig / split_info if split_info > 0 else 0.0

print()
for f in ["row_id", "useful", "coarse"]:
    print(f"gain ratio({f:8s}) = {gain_ratio(df2, f):.4f}")
# The ID column's advantage collapses -- this is what C4.5 added to ID3.

# =====================================================================
# 7. ID3 (multiway) vs CART (binary)
# =====================================================================
print(f"\nID3 would split Outlook into {data.Outlook.nunique()} branches at once")
t = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(f"CART builds a BINARY tree: {t.tree_.node_count} nodes, "
      f"{t.get_n_leaves()} leaves, depth {t.get_depth()}")
print("every internal node has exactly 2 children:",
      all((t.tree_.children_left[i] == -1) == (t.tree_.children_right[i] == -1)
          for i in range(t.tree_.node_count)))
# Binary splits can REVISIT the same feature deeper in the tree, which uses
# the data far more efficiently than exhausting it in one multiway split.

# =====================================================================
# 8. THE TWO CRITERIA RARELY DISAGREE
# =====================================================================
Xb = rng.normal(0, 1, (2000, 10))
yb = (Xb[:, 0] + Xb[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, 2000) > 0).astype(int)
for crit in ["gini", "entropy"]:
    s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion=crit, max_depth=5,
                                               random_state=0), Xb, yb, cv=5)
    print(f"criterion={crit:8s} cv accuracy {s.mean():.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")

items:
Entropy $=-\sum_c p_c\log_2 p_c$. Range $[0,1]$ for two
 classes: $0$ is pure, $1$ is max impure. It measures
 how mixed or impure the data is in a node — high entropy is an
 unordered deck, low entropy an ordered one.

Gini $=1-\sum_c p_c^2$. Range $[0,0.5]$:
 conceptually the same as entropy at node level, only the formulas
 differ.

Gini performs better on big datasets — entropy has a log so it
 takes more time; the Gini formula is simple math.

Information Gain $=H(S)-\sum_v\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)$ —
 it measures how good a feature is at reducing the entropy.
 Whichever feature has higher IG, use that to split.
 The tree chooses the split with the largest entropy reduction.

The child impurities are weighted by size, so a pure child of two
 rows counts for little.

The Outlook example: $H(\text{root})=0.940$, weighted children $0.694$,
 $IG=0.247$ — the highest of the four features, so the tree splits there.
 Overcast is a pure split and becomes a leaf.

ID3: classification only, multiway, rare, entropy/IG.
 CART: both tasks, strictly binary, very common —
 the basis of Random Forest — Gini for classification,
 MSE/variance for regression.

Information gain is biased towards high-cardinality features;
 gain ratio and binary splitting are the two fixes.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

The average number of yes/no questions needed to identify the class of a random
member of the node. Zero when the node is pure — you already know — and one bit
when the classes are evenly split. That is why the logarithm is base 2.

Practically it rarely matters — the two curves have nearly the same shape and
almost always select the same split. Gini is the default because it avoids the
logarithm and is therefore faster on large datasets. Entropy has the cleaner
information-theoretic interpretation.
Q. Why is the child impurity weighted by $|S_v|/|S|$?

Because a perfectly pure child containing two rows is worth much less than a
nearly pure child containing two hundred. Without the weights the algorithm would
prefer splits that isolate tiny accidental groups.
Q. Can information gain be negative?

No. A split can never increase the weighted average impurity of the children, so
$IG\ge0$. A gain of exactly zero means the split conveys no information about the
target.
Q. Why does information gain favour a unique ID column?

Because a feature with $n$ distinct values can split $n$ rows into $n$
single-element groups, every one of which is trivially pure. The gain equals the
root entropy — the maximum possible — and the feature predicts nothing on new
data. Gain ratio penalises this by dividing by the split information; CART's
binary splits mitigate it structurally.
Q. ID3 or CART — what is the practical difference?

ID3 does classification only, builds multiway trees and uses entropy with
information gain. CART does both classification and regression, builds strictly
binary trees, and uses Gini or MSE. CART is what scikit-learn implements and what
random forests and boosting are built on — binary splits use the data more
efficiently because the same feature can be revisited deeper in the tree.
